source.title: The Double Descent Behavior in Two Layer Neural Network for Binary Classification
source.authors: Chathurika S. Abeykoon; A. Beknazaryan; Hai-Lin Sang

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates double-descent-related test-error behavior using a two-layer binary classifier and a different, ratio-wise setup; it also reports a sample-size sweep on a real dataset.
record.gate_note: The theoretical results vary α=n/d, not model size with n and d fixed, and therefore do not test model-wise double descent. The paper does not vary training epochs. The Wisconsin Breast Cancer experiment does vary training sample size with feature dimension fixed and reports test error. Theoretical α-sweep findings are recorded under fits_no_version because α changes the sample-size/dimension ratio rather than isolating the sample-size axis.
record.test_reason: The study derives CGMT test-error curves for a single-ReLU-unit binary classifier as a function of α=n/d. Since p=d, sweeping α at fixed d is a sample-wise sweep, and its inverse is a capacity sweep. It also runs one fixed-dimension sample-size sweep on Wisconsin Breast Cancer at two regularization strengths. These results bear on V3, on V6's regularization part, and loosely on V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, with two additions. The authors frame the result as ratio-wise double descent, with the peak at n=d and the best error in the underparameterized region. They conclude that suitable l2 regularization (about 0.1–1, or λ=5 for equal classes) removes the peak and gives a monotone decrease consistent with 'more data is always better'; too-strong λ hurts when classes are unequal.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a CGMT-based theoretical analysis of a two-layer binary classifier and varies α = n/d; it also includes a sample-size sweep on Wisconsin Breast Cancer. It does not reproduce the original model-capacity sweep with n and d fixed.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curve changes with regularization strength and class balance ρ₁; at ρ₁ = 0.7, strong regularization delays the reported decline to larger α.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed α=4 and α=7, error as a function of λ is minimized at a finite λ* when ρ₁≠0.5. At ρ₁=0.5 it stays low beyond λ*.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this classifier, the optimal regularization strength is finite and depends on class imbalance.

record.code_released: not stated; R/RStudio code is included in supplementary material
record.problems: The theoretical result is ratio-wise and is not a direct test of model-wise, epoch-wise, or isolated sample-wise double descent. The empirical sample-size experiment is on one dataset and the prose's 10-hidden-neuron description conflicts with supplementary code specifying 30 units. Curves are reported without uncertainty estimates. The authors state that they do not use an iterative training algorithm for the theoretical results.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results were omitted.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep in a deep network with n and d fixed.
No epoch-wise test-error sweep. Section 2 asserts epochs matter but shows no results.
Model classes other than this single-ReLU-unit classifier are not studied.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict peak location.
Label noise is not varied, multiple or triple peaks are not examined, and no per-α optimally tuned λ curve is computed.

missing.what: Low-regularization curves at ρ₁=0.7, where the text says double descent is 'clearly observed' (start error 0.3). No row records them.
The authors' recommendation of λ=5 for equal classes and 0.1≤λ≤1 overall, the basis for their claim that optimal regularization removes the peak.

record.verdict_notes: The 'two-layer network' in the theory is a single ReLU unit on xᵀβ/√d, effectively a linear classifier, so it is not a deep network. The empirical curve is a single run, with test BCE loss as the metric and dropout 0.3 in the code. The study is not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: Model size is not varied with training sample size and dimension held fixed.
Training epochs are not varied in a test-error sweep.
The direct sample-size result is the Wisconsin Breast Cancer experiment; the theoretical α sweeps do not isolate increasing sample size at fixed dimension.
The study examines a two-layer neural network, not double descent across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across axes.
Regularization effects are examined, but label noise, multiple/triple peaks, and whether optimally tuned regularization removes peaks across settings are not comprehensively tested.
The study does not re-express complexity using an effective parameter count to test whether the curve becomes an ordinary U.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU model
rows.size_stated: one hidden layer with 10 neurons in the Section 2 description; the supplementary code specifies 30 units
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of training samples while keeping the feature dimension fixed and measured test error.
rows.value: The error decreases, shows a slight increase around α = 1, and decreases again.
rows.note: The paper describes the increase as slight. The stated model size conflicts with the supplementary code, which builds a 30-unit hidden layer.
rows.check: Only a 'slight increase' around α=1. Single seed, no uncertainty. The plotted 'test error' is the Keras BCE test loss, not misclassification. The code uses 30 hidden units plus dropout 0.3, not the 10 units in the prose. α=1 is n equal to the 30 input features, not the network's parameter-count interpolation threshold (~990 parameters).

source_check.problem: The qualitative result matches. The paper's prose specifies 10 hidden neurons, while its code specifies 30; the reported empirical metric is evaluated loss.

rows.note: This is a setting where the reported sample-size sweep does not show a rise near α = 1. The stated model size conflicts with the supplementary code, which builds a 30-unit hidden layer.
rows.check: No rise near α=1 at λ=0.1. This also bears on V6: regularization removes the peak. Same metric and architecture caveats as r1.

rows.subject: model (3.1), two-layer ReLU neural network
rows.size_stated: p = d; n and d tend to infinity with α = n/d fixed
rows.operation_detail: Computed theoretical test error as a function of the sample-size-to-dimension ratio α.
rows.value: It first decreases, rises to a peak at α = 1, then decreases for α > 1.
rows.note: This is the paper's ratio-wise result; it does not isolate model-size growth or sample-size growth with dimension fixed.
rows.check: Should not be 'none'. With p=d, increasing α at fixed d means more samples, and error rises to a peak at α=1 (n=d). Read inversely (d/n), error falls again past interpolation. Caveats: theoretical asymptotics, λ=10⁻⁵, a single-neuron model (essentially a linear classifier), not a deep network.

rows.value: The error remains unchanged until a specific α, then decreases monotonically as α increases.
rows.note: The reported curve has a plateau followed by a decline rather than a stated peak.

statements.correction: Wisconsin Breast Cancer; λ=0.1; Figure 3 reports monotonic decrease with α=n/d in both parameterization regions; empirical plotted metric is evaluated binary-cross-entropy loss.
Square-loss theory; ρ₁=0.7; λ≥1 produces an initial plateau followed by decline; λ=100 begins declining around α≈60; stronger regularization delays improvement.
Unequal class probabilities; strong regularization removes the peak while delaying error reduction; Section 6.2 recommends suitable regularization rather than arbitrarily large λ.
